# Overview

Study 3 takes the tokens whose surprisal exceeds τ = 11.28 bits and asks
what kind of unconventionality they contain. Two representations are reported.

- **δ components (the proposal's method).** δ = e_pred − e_obs in OLMo-2 1B's
  output space, decomposed by NMF (k = 50) on dev essays.
- **LM repairs (added after the premise checks).** The language model scores
  about 23 minimal edits at each token, and the best edit, or NONE, names the
  problem. It was chosen in the representation lab (`lab/README.md`) as the only
  representation that meets all four pre-set criteria on a held-out synthetic
  benchmark.

Everything that touches proficiency labels was fixed before the test set was
read (`DECISIONS.md`, D11). Results are reported by research question.
Companion reports are `premises.qmd` (what the selected tokens are, and why δ
is mostly word identity) and `lab/README.md` (how the repair representation
was found).

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)
source("src/1-predictability-benchmark/_viz_helpers.R")
R3 <- "results/study3"
S3 <- "src/3-vector-transformations"
labels <- read_csv(file.path(S3, "component_labels.csv"))
comps <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "components_delta.csv")) |> left_join(select(labels, -top_lemma_share), by = "component")
cors_test <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "component_correlations_test.csv")) |> left_join(select(labels, -top_lemma_share), by = "component")
sweep <- list.files(R3, "^nmf_ksweep_\\d+\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) |> map_dfr(read_csv)
```

# RQ1. Do the errors decompose into interpretable components?

## δ components

```{r}
#| label: sweep
sweep |>
  group_by(k) |>
  summarise(seeds = n(), median_matched_cos = paste(sprintf("%.3f", median_matched_cos), collapse = " / "),
            rel_error = mean(rel_error), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Split-half stability (two essay-level split seeds) and reconstruction error. k = 80 seed 1 did not converge, so the D4 rule selects k = 50")
```

```{r}
#| label: taxonomy
comps |>
  count(class, level) |>
  arrange(class, desc(n)) |>
  kable(caption = "Taxonomy of the 50 δ components (D5/D10)")
comps |>
  filter(class != "lexeme feature") |>
  select(component, class, level, label, top_observed, top_predicted, top_lemma_share) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "The ten components that are not single-word features")
```

Forty of the fifty components are a single observed word: a top-lemma share
of ≥ .50 among the 200 highest-loading tokens, and usually 1.00. The
decomposition recovers a vocabulary partition, which the premise checks
predicted. Of the remaining ten, three are artifacts: subword continuation
after a word fragment, punctuation spacing, and the corpus's anonymization
placeholders. Seven were labelled error patterns, and every one of them is
defined by what the model *expected* (*the*, *to*, *be*, *is*), not by what was
written. Section RQ2 shows that at least two of those seven are better read as
lexical range than as error.

## LM repairs on real essays

```{r}
#| label: repair-dist
byband <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "repair_label_by_band.csv"))
byband |>
  group_by(label) |>
  summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Best repair after the edit cost, dev ELLIPSE tokens above τ")
```

A third of selected tokens get NONE: no single-word edit pays for itself. Two
broad classes, *replace content word* and *delete content word*, take another
28%. The named grammatical edits share the rest: spelling (non-word and
real-word), inflection, function-word replacement, insertion and deletion. KWIC
cards for every label are in `results/study3/repair_cards.md`. The winning edit
is the proposed correction, as these dev examples show:

- non-word spelling: *atitude → attitude*, *thier → their*, *hellp → help*;
- real-word confusion: *thing → think*, *Specially → especially*;
- inflection: *know → knew*, *described → describes*, *a street that look →
  looks*, *I have choose → chosen*;
- omission: *have [a] sort of*, *as [a] result*, *never too late [to] fix*,
  *extend the day [by] two hours*.

### Check against the blinded hand coding

The 150 tokens coded before either representation existed (premises §3,
D7) give a real-data test of the D8 predictions.

```{r}
#| label: coded
k <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "repair_coded.csv")) |> filter(code != "OTHER") |>
  mutate(op = if_else(label == "NONE", "NONE", str_extract(label, "^[A-Z]+")))
k |>
  group_by(code) |>
  summarise(n = n(), pays = mean(label != "NONE"), net_gain_median = median(net_gain),
            insertion = mean(op == "INS"), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Coded tokens: share with a paying edit, median net gain (bits), share whose best edit is an insertion")
auc <- function(score, y) { r <- rank(score); n1 <- sum(y); (sum(r[y]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * sum(!y)) }
kk <- k
```

Both predictions hold. Errors get a paying edit more often than acceptable
tokens (E_TOK 92%, E_CTX 84%, OK 53%). Insertion is the best edit for 30% of
E_CTX tokens, where the error is an omission just before the word, and for 2% of
E_TOK tokens. Net gain separates errors from acceptable tokens with AUC
`r sprintf("%.2f", auc(kk$net_gain, kk$code != "OK"))`, and surprisal itself
manages `r sprintf("%.2f", auc(kk$surprisal_bits, kk$code != "OK"))` on the same
tokens. Every coded token is already above τ, so surprisal has little
range left here. That is exactly the situation the repair representation is
meant for.

# RQ2. Are components differentially associated with proficiency?

```{r}
#| label: rq2
ov <- cors_test |> filter(score == "overall")
fig <- ov |>
  mutate(name = sprintf("C%02d %s", component, str_trunc(label, 48)),
         sig = if_else(q < .05, "q < .05", "n.s.")) |>
  ggplot(aes(rho, fct_reorder(name, rho), colour = class, shape = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`q < .05` = 16, n.s. = 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`lexeme feature` = "grey50", `error pattern` = "#b2182b", artifact = "#56B4E9"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Spearman ρ with Overall (prompt-centred, test essays)", y = NULL) +
  theme_study1(10)
save_fig(fig, "rq2_components", 8, 9, dir = R3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rq2
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 9
fig
h2 <- fromJSON(file.path(R3, "h2_permutation_test.json"))
```

On test, `r sum(ov$q < .05)` of 50 components correlate with Overall at q <
.05. The frozen H2 test compares mean |ρ| between the morphosyntactic error
patterns and the content-word lexeme features: `r sprintf("%.3f", h2$mean_abs_rho_morphosyntactic)`
vs `r sprintf("%.3f", h2$mean_abs_rho_lexical)`, permutation p =
`r sprintf("%.3f", h2$p_one_sided)` (5 vs 27 components). It replicates the dev
result (p = .019).

The test passes, but H2 as worded is not supported. H2 says morphosyntactic
components load disproportionately on *low*-proficiency essays, and |ρ|
ignores direction. Three of the five morphosyntactic components correlate
*positively* with Overall: C0, determiner expected before a noun, ρ = +.33;
C4, *be* expected, +.13; and C12, *the* expected, +.10. Only C8
(*have/do/make* for the copula, −.22) and C13 (*to* omitted, −.09) load on
weak essays. C0's cards explain the reversal. Many of its tokens are correct
zero-article generic plurals and rarer nouns (*about teenagers*, *freshmen*,
*kidnapped*), which strong writers produce more often. The component marks
lexical range at a position where the model expected a determiner, not
omission. The labels were written blind to outcomes and stay as frozen, and
this reading is reported as a post-hoc interpretation.

The repair labels behave differently (exploratory, test essays).

```{r}
#| label: repair-direction
prof <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "profiles_ellipse_repair.csv.gz"))
pc <- function(df, col) { m <- df |> filter(split == "dev") |> group_by(prompt) |> summarise(m = mean(.data[[col]])); df[[col]] - m$m[match(df$prompt, m$prompt)] }
te <- prof$split == "test"
y <- pc(prof, "overall")
rr <- grep("^rr_", names(prof), value = TRUE)
rep_dir <- tibble(label = sub("^rr_", "", rr),
                  rho = map_dbl(rr, ~ cor(pc(prof, .x)[te], y[te], method = "spearman")),
                  per_1000 = map_dbl(rr, ~ 1000 * mean(prof[[.x]][te]))) |> arrange(rho)
kable(rep_dir, digits = 3, caption = "Per-token rate of each repair label vs. Overall (prompt-centred, test). Exploratory")
```

Every repair label is more frequent in weaker essays, and none is meaningfully
positive. That is what a measure of error should show. The δ components
point in both directions because many of them encode vocabulary rather than
error.

# RQ3. Do profiles add information beyond mean surprisal?

```{r}
#| label: rq3
lad <- bind_rows(read_csv(file.path(R3, "ladder_devcv.csv")), read_csv(file.path(R3, "ladder_test.csv")))
lad |>
  mutate(est = if_else(str_detect(model, " - "), r2, delta_r2_vs_B0),
         cell = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", est, ci_lo, ci_hi),
         cell = if_else(model == "B0", sprintf("R² = %.3f", r2), cell)) |>
  select(model, mode, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = mode, values_from = cell) |>
  kable(caption = "ΔR² over B0 (mean surprisal + log length), within-prompt; contrast rows give the difference between the two named models. devcv = 10-fold prompt-grouped CV within dev; test = fit on dev, scored once on test, 2,000 bootstrap resamples")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rq3
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
p <- lad |>
  filter(!str_detect(model, " - "), model != "B0") |>
  mutate(model = fct_reorder(model, delta_r2_vs_B0)) |>
  ggplot(aes(delta_r2_vs_B0, model, colour = mode)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, .05), colour = c("grey60", "grey80"), linetype = c(1, 2)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), size = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(devcv = "#ef8a62", test = "#2166ac"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "ΔR² over mean surprisal + length", y = NULL) +
  theme_study1()
save_fig(p, "rq3_ladder", 8, 4, dir = R3)
p
```

Under the frozen rules:

- **H3 is supported for the δ profile.** On test, ΔR² = .062 [.048, .076]:
  the point estimate is above .05 and the lower bound above zero.
- **The increment is not evidence of error types (D3).** The observed-word
  profile M_obs does as well (M − M_obs = .001 [−.008, .010]). Whatever the
  high-surprisal tokens add to mean surprisal is available from *which words*
  were surprising.
- **The repair profile does about as well.** R = .051 [.035, .066]. In dev it
  edged ahead of δ (+.019), and on test it did not (−.011 [−.029, .006]).
- **Both add a little to the Study 2 battery.** S2+M − S2 = .014 and S2+R − S2
  = .012, with both lower bounds above zero.
- **Distributional summaries add almost nothing** (B1: surprisal variance and
  rate above τ).

Prediction does not choose between the representations. Interpretation does.
At equal predictive power, the repair profile's dimensions are named,
directional edits. The δ profile is mostly a vocabulary profile.

# RQ4. Alignment with the analytic ratings (exploratory)

```{r}
#| label: rq4
cors_test |>
  filter(score != "overall") |>
  group_by(level, score) |>
  summarise(mean_abs_partial = mean(abs(rho_partial_overall)), n = n_distinct(component), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = score, values_from = mean_abs_partial) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "δ components: mean |ρ| with each analytic score after partialling Overall, by component level (test)")
```

```{r}
#| label: rq4-repair
an <- c("cohesion", "syntax", "vocabulary", "phraseology", "grammar", "conventions")
o <- y[te]
part <- function(v) { v <- v[te]; resid(lm(v ~ o)) }
rep4 <- expand_grid(label = rr, score = an) |>
  mutate(rho = map2_dbl(label, score, ~ cor(part(pc(prof, .x)), part(pc(prof, .y)), method = "spearman")),
         label = sub("^rr_", "", label))
p4 <- rep4 |>
  filter(label %in% (rep_dir |> filter(per_1000 > 1) |> pull(label))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(score, an), fct_rev(label), fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", rho)), size = 2.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#b2182b", high = "#2166ac", mid = "white", limits = c(-.2, .2), oob = scales::squish) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "partial ρ") +
  theme_study1(10)
save_fig(p4, "rq4_repair_heatmap", 7, 6, dir = R3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rq4
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
p4
```

Once Overall is partialled out, what is left is small, which is expected
given how strongly the six analytic scores correlate. The δ components with the
clearest residual alignment are orthographic (misspellings, punctuation
spacing) with Conventions. The heat map gives the same reading for the repair
labels that occur at least once per 1,000 tokens. Negative cells mean the
edit is more frequent than Overall alone predicts in essays rated lower on
that trait.

```{r}

ph
```

The heat map is the Study 1 fairness procedure applied to each repair label:
within-level Cohen's d, focal L1 vs all others, averaged across levels
weighted by focal-group size. Positive (red) means the edit is more frequent
for that L1 than for others at the same level. |d| ≥ .20 is the descriptive
flag.

# RQ6. Errors and acceptable surprise

This section was added after RQ1–RQ5 (D13, D15–D17). It asks how much of an
essay's high surprisal is error and how much is an acceptable but unexpected
word choice. Gold labels come from the expert edits in W&I+LOCNESS
(Yannakoudakis et al. 2018; LOCNESS courtesy of CECL, Louvain).

- **Model.** A token classifier (gradient boosting) gives P(acceptable) for
  each token above τ. It is trained on W&I train only, and combines three
  kinds of label-free evidence: the LM repair scores, Dolma attestation of the
  word and its neighbours, and how the word's surprisal changes under more
  context, a larger model and a bidirectional model.
- **Essay rates.** For each essay, the error rate is the sum of
  1 − P(acceptable) over its high tokens, divided by its token count. The
  acceptable rate is the sum of P(acceptable) divided by the same count.
- **Prior adjustment.** Summing probabilities is biased when an essay's base
  rate differs from the training base rate, so the main estimates use a
  per-essay EM prior adjustment (Saerens et al. 2002; D16). Unadjusted
  estimates are shown alongside.

```{r}
#| label: accept-confirm
sb <- read_csv("results/study3/lab/accept_scoreboard.csv") |>
  filter(mode %in% c("dev_gbm", "confirm_gbm"),
         rep %in% c("surprisal", "ctx_excess_s4", "att_full_s", "rep_mdl_plus_pos", "comb_rac")) |>
  group_by(rep, mode) |> slice_tail(n = 1) |> ungroup() |>
  select(rep, mode, auc_err_ok, auc_ins_ok, prec_ok_at_50, auc_A, auc_B, auc_C) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = mode, values_from = auc_err_ok:auc_C) |>
  mutate(rep = recode(rep, surprisal = "surprisal and entropy", ctx_excess_s4 = "context and capacity views",
                      att_full_s = "attestation", rep_mdl_plus_pos = "repair",
                      comb_rac = "repair + attestation + context")) |>
  arrange(auc_err_ok_confirm_gbm)
sb |> select(rep, `dev CV` = auc_err_ok_dev_gbm, `held out` = auc_err_ok_confirm_gbm,
             `omissions, held out` = auc_ins_ok_confirm_gbm, `precision of the top half` = prec_ok_at_50_confirm_gbm,
             A = auc_A_confirm_gbm, B = auc_B_confirm_gbm, C = auc_C_confirm_gbm) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Token-level AUC for error vs acceptable among W&I tokens above τ. Held out is W&I dev; the OK base rate is .63.")
```

The combined model was fixed before the held-out run. Its held-out AUC equals
its development estimate, and it is close to flat across CEFR levels.

```{r}
#| label: wi-levels
dt <- fromJSON("results/study3/decompose_tests.json")
wl <- map_dfr(names(dt$wi_heldout_by_level), \(m) tibble(measure = m, level = names(dt$wi_heldout_by_level[[m]]),
                                                         value = unlist(dt$wi_heldout_by_level[[m]])))
wl |> mutate(value = 1000 * value) |> pivot_wider(names_from = level) |>
  mutate(measure = recode(measure, n_high_rate = "all tokens above τ", err_rate = "errors, unadjusted",
                          acc_rate = "acceptable, unadjusted", err_em_rate = "errors, EM",
                          acc_em_rate = "acceptable, EM", g_err_rate = "errors, gold", g_ok_rate = "acceptable, gold")) |>
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "W&I dev and LOCNESS (held out): rate per 1,000 tokens by level. N = native (LOCNESS). Gold excludes tokens that follow an error (POST).")
```

Two things stand out.

- **Natives are more surprising than C learners**, not less, and the
  difference is acceptable surprise. Their error rate is the same as C's.
- **The unadjusted acceptable rate is flat across A–C**, while the gold rate
  rises. The EM-adjusted rate follows gold.

```{r}
#| label: ellipse-rates
rho_tab <- function(r, sfx) {
  tibble(rate = c("all above τ", "errors", "acceptable", "acceptable share of high", "rare attested, acceptable"),
         key = c("high_rate", paste0(c("err_rate", "acc_rate", "acc_share", "acc_rare_attested_rate"), sfx))) |>
    mutate(rho = map_dbl(key, \(k) r[[paste0("rho_", k, "_overall")]]),
           lo = map_dbl(key, \(k) r[[paste0("ci_", k, "_overall")]][1]),
           hi = map_dbl(key, \(k) r[[paste0("ci_", k, "_overall")]][2]))
}
rt <- bind_rows(rho_tab(dt$test, "") |> mutate(version = "unadjusted"),
                rho_tab(dt$test_em, "_em") |> mutate(version = "EM"))
rt |> transmute(version, rate, `ρ with Overall` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", rho, lo, hi)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = version, values_from = `ρ with Overall`) |>
  kable(caption = "ELLIPSE test (n = 1,945): Spearman ρ of each essay rate with Overall, 95% bootstrap CI")
```

```{r}
#| label: coded-check
cc <- read_csv("results/study3/decompose_coded_check.csv") |> mutate(band = factor(band, c("low", "mid", "high")))
pcc <- cc |>
  select(band, acc_rate, acc_rate_em, acc_rate_coded, err_rate_em, err_rate_coded) |>
  pivot_longer(-band) |>
  mutate(kind = if_else(str_starts(name, "acc"), "acceptable", "error"),
         source = case_when(str_ends(name, "coded") ~ "blind hand coding", str_ends(name, "em") ~ "model, EM",
                            TRUE ~ "model, unadjusted")) |>
  ggplot(aes(band, 1000 * value, colour = source, group = interaction(source, kind), linetype = kind)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`blind hand coding` = "black", `model, EM` = "#b2182b", `model, unadjusted` = "grey60")) +
  labs(x = "Overall tertile (ELLIPSE dev)", y = "Per 1,000 tokens", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_study1()
save_fig(pcc, "rq6_coded_check", 7, 4, dir = R3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-coded-check
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
pcc
```

The hand-coded line is an independent check on ELLIPSE itself, from the
blinded premise sample (50 tokens per tertile, coded before any of this
modelling). The coded acceptable share is multiplied by each tertile's rate of
tokens above τ. The unadjusted model gets the direction of the acceptable rate
wrong, and the EM version gets it right.

```{r}
#| label: tests-a
tibble(test = c("A1. errors track Overall more strongly than all high tokens (Δρ)",
                "A2. |ρ acceptable| − |ρ errors|",
                "A4. CV R², Overall from all high tokens",
                "A4. CV R², Overall from errors + acceptable"),
       unadjusted = c(sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", dt$test$A1_diff, dt$test$A1_ci[1], dt$test$A1_ci[2]),
                      sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", dt$test$A2_diff, dt$test$A2_ci[1], dt$test$A2_ci[2]),
                      sprintf("%.3f", dt$test$A4_r2_high), sprintf("%.3f", dt$test$A4_r2_split)),
       EM = c(sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", dt$test_em$A1_diff, dt$test_em$A1_ci[1], dt$test_em$A1_ci[2]),
              sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", dt$test_em$A2_diff, dt$test_em$A2_ci[1], dt$test_em$A2_ci[2]),
              sprintf("%.3f", dt$test_em$A4_r2_high), sprintf("%.3f", dt$test_em$A4_r2_split))) |>
  kable(caption = "Pre-specified tests on ELLIPSE test (D15)")

a3 <- bind_rows(
  enframe(unlist(dt$test_em[str_starts(names(dt$test_em), "A3_")])) |> mutate(name = str_remove(name, "^A3_"))) |>
  separate_wider_regex(name, c(rate = ".*_em", "_", trait = "[a-z]+")) |>
  mutate(rate = recode(rate, err_rate_em = "errors", acc_rate_em = "acceptable",
                       acc_rare_attested_rate_em = "rare attested")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = trait)
a3 |> kable(digits = 2, caption = "A3 (exploratory): partial Spearman ρ with each analytic score, controlling Overall, ELLIPSE test, EM rates")
```

TOEFL 11 replicates the ELLIPSE pattern with nothing fit on it. All tokens
above τ give ρ = −.38 with level. EM errors give −.61, and the EM acceptable
rate gives +.52.

## What this says about "creativity"

- **Acceptable surprise is real and rises with proficiency.** Errors fall
  faster, so the total amount of surprise still falls. On ELLIPSE, the
  EM-adjusted rate of acceptable unexpected words rises from about 2 to
  about 5 per 100 tokens across the Overall tertiles, while errors fall from
  about 15 to 5.
- **Native writers produce the most acceptable surprise.** Their errors are
  at the C-level rate, so the extra surprise in their essays is the
  acceptable kind.
- **Acceptable surprise is a secondary part of the proficiency signal.**
  - Errors correlate more strongly with Overall than acceptable surprise
    does (A2).
  - Controlling for Overall, acceptable surprise relates about as much to
    Grammar and Conventions as to Vocabulary. Part of the adjusted rate
    reflects how error-free the essay is.
  - The cleaner lexical index, acceptable mass on rare words attested in
    Dolma, is most specific to Vocabulary, but its partial correlation is
    small (.10).
- **The decomposition improves prediction.** Splitting the high-surprisal
  count into its two parts raises the CV R² for Overall from .33 to .45.

So the measure does not penalize unexpected-but-acceptable writing. The
penalty comes from errors, and acceptable surprise counts in the writer's
favour once it is separated out. Whether acceptable surprise is *effective*
writing is not something the gold labels can show, since W&I edits mark
errors, not quality.

# Summary for the write-up

- **RQ1.** The δ decomposition is stable (split-half median matched cosine
  ≥ .99) but recovers a vocabulary partition: 40 of 50 components are single
  observed words. This follows from δ's construction. The LM repair
  representation names the problem at each token, and usually the correction
  too. On real tokens coded blind, it separates errors from acceptable words
  (AUC above surprisal's), and it recognizes omissions as insertions.
- **RQ2.** Components differ in their association with proficiency, and the
  frozen H2 |ρ| test passes. The directional claim fails for δ: three of the
  five morphosyntactic components rise with proficiency. Every repair label
  falls with proficiency.
- **RQ3.** H3 is supported for the δ profile (ΔR² = .062). The increment is
  equally available from the observed words alone, and the repair profile adds
  as much. Prediction does not discriminate between representations.
- **RQ4.** Residual alignment with specific analytic scores is small. The
  clearest is orthographic components with Conventions.
- **RQ5.** The pre-registered article test is supported. Insert-determiner
  repairs are more frequent for L1s without articles (0.36 within-level SD,
  p < .0001). The δ components do not replicate on TOEFL.
- **RQ6.** A classifier trained on gold W&I edits separates errors from
  acceptable words above τ (held-out AUC .87, against .68 for surprisal).
  Splitting each essay's surprisal into errors and acceptable surprise shows
  two opposite trends. Errors fall steeply with proficiency, and acceptable
  surprise rises. This replicates on TOEFL 11. Native writers have the most
  acceptable surprise.
